# zuint

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuint/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuint/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zuint/gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuint/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Overview

R has 32-bit integers and doubles, and a double is exact only up to
2^53^. Databases and data files have more: Arrow and Parquet have signed and
unsigned 64-bit integers, and DuckDB adds 128-bit ones. Read into R, an
unsigned ID or a `HUGEINT` becomes a double and quietly loses its low
digits, and writing it back loses the column's type as well.

zuint gives R the four integer types those engines use, `int64`, `uint64`,
`int128` and `uint128`, and moves them in and out of Arrow, Parquet and
DuckDB with every value and every column type intact.

* **Exact or explicit.** A result is exact, or it is `NA` with a warning, or
  an error. Nothing is rounded, truncated or clamped without saying so, and
  nothing is compared through a double.
* **Overflow is a choice.** Operators give `NA` with a warning, as R's
  integers do; `checked_*()` functions raise an error and `wrapping_*()`
  functions compute modulo 2^64^ or 2^128^.
* **Types mix without loss.** Combining two types gives the smallest type
  that holds both, so `int64` and `uint64` meet in `int128`; where there is
  no such type, it is an error.
* **Compatible with bit64.** `int64` is a bit64 `integer64` underneath, so
  data.table, arrow, duckdb and the database drivers read it as they read
  `integer64`.
* **One bridge to the engines.** Data moves through the
  [Arrow C Data Interface](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/CDataInterface.html),
  in C, with no R package in between; nanoarrow, arrow and duckdb are only
  needed for their own conveniences.

| Engine type | R today | zuint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arrow `int64`, DuckDB `BIGINT` | a double by default, or bit64 `integer64` | `int64` |
| Arrow `uint64`, DuckDB `UBIGINT` | a double, rounded beyond 2^53^ | `uint64` |
| DuckDB `HUGEINT` | a double | `int128` |
| DuckDB `UHUGEINT` | a double | `uint128` |

## Installation

zuint is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zuint")
```

## Usage

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zuint)
```

A number beyond 2^53^ is exact, where a double has already rounded it:

```{r}
x <- uint64("18446744073709551614")
x
x - 1L
sprintf("%.0f", 18446744073709551614 - 1)
```

An out-of-range result is `NA` with a warning, unless you choose another
overflow policy:

```{r}
big <- int64("9223372036854775807")
big + 1L
try(checked_add(big, 1L))
wrapping_mul(x, 31L)
```

Mixing types never loses a value: an `int64` and a `uint64` give an `int128`,
and a product too large for `int64` fits in `int128`:

```{r}
int64(-1) + uint64("18446744073709551614")
int128(big) * 4L
```

Values come out of DuckDB as they are stored, and go back with their types.
Here a `UHUGEINT` near the top of its range makes the round trip:

```{r}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
ids <- zu_duckdb_query(
  con,
  "SELECT 340282366920938463463374607431768211454::UHUGEINT AS id"
)
ids$id

zu_duckdb_register(con, "ids_back", ids)
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT typeof(id) AS type, id::VARCHAR AS id FROM ids_back")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

Text goes both ways in decimal, hexadecimal and binary:

```{r}
format_hex(uint64("0xdead_beef"))
format_bin(int64(-5))
format(int64(1234567890123), big.mark = ",")
```

The constructors are named after the types, and every conversion into a
type, from a double, a string or another type, follows the same rule: exact,
or `NA` with a warning.

## Learn more

* The [reference index](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuint/reference/) lists
  every function, with the type ranges in `?int64`, the overflow policies in
  `?checked_add` and the Arrow bridge in `?zu_from_arrow`.

## Related work

[bit64](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bit64) gave R its 64-bit integers
and the `integer64` layout that zuint's `int64` keeps. The 128-bit
arithmetic, parsing and formatting come from
[zufast](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zufast). Arrow arrays move through the
Arrow C Data Interface, and the 128-bit types through DuckDB's
`arrow.opaque` extension types. The tests check values against
[gmp](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=gmp).
